{{Short description | Measure of curve's deviation; invariant under transformations}}
In [[differential geometry]], the '''total absolute curvature''' of a [[smooth curve]] is a number defined by integrating the [[absolute value]] of the [[curvature]] around the curve. It is a [[dimensionless quantity]] that is [[Invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] under [[Similarity (geometry)|similarity transformation]]s of the curve, and that can be used to measure how far the curve is from being a [[convex curve]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Brook | first1 = Alexander
 | last2 = Bruckstein | first2 = Alfred M. |author2-link= Alfred Marcel Bruckstein
 | last3 = Kimmel | first3 = Ron | author3-link = Ron Kimmel
 | editor1-last = Kimmel | editor1-first = Ron | editor1-link = Ron Kimmel
 | editor2-last = Sochen | editor2-first = Nir A.
 | editor3-last = Weickert | editor3-first = Joachim
 | contribution = On similarity-invariant fairness measures
 | doi = 10.1007/11408031_39
 | pages = 456–467
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | title = Scale Space and PDE Methods in Computer Vision: 5th International Conference, Scale-Space 2005, Hofgeismar, Germany, April 7-9, 2005, Proceedings
 | volume = 3459
 | year = 2005| isbn = 978-3-540-25547-5
 }}.</ref>

If the curve is parameterized by its [[arc length]], the total absolute curvature can be expressed by the formula
:<math>\int |\kappa(s)| ds,</math>
where {{mvar|s}} is the arc length parameter and {{mvar|&kappa;}} is the curvature.
This is almost the same as the formula for the [[total curvature]], but differs in using the absolute value instead of the signed curvature.<ref name="chen">{{citation
 | last = Chen | first = Bang-Yen
 | contribution = Riemannian submanifolds
 | doi = 10.1016/S1874-5741(00)80006-0
 | mr = 1736854
 | pages = 187–418
 | publisher = North-Holland, Amsterdam
 | title = Handbook of differential geometry, Vol. I
 | year = 2000| volume = 1
 | isbn = 978-0-444-82240-6
 }}. See in particular section 21.1, "Rotation index and total curvature of a curve", [https://books.google.com/books?id=U2BIz8NNksYC&pg=PA359 pp.&nbsp;359–360].</ref>

Because the total curvature of a [[Jordan curve theorem|simple closed curve]] in the [[Euclidean plane]] is always exactly 2{{pi}}, the total ''absolute'' curvature of a simple closed curve is also always ''at least'' 2{{pi}}. It is exactly 2{{pi}} for a [[convex curve]], and greater than 2{{pi}} whenever the curve has any non-convexities.<ref name="chen"/> When a smooth simple closed curve undergoes the [[curve-shortening flow]], its total absolute curvature decreases monotonically until the curve becomes convex, after which its total absolute curvature remains fixed at 2{{pi}} until the curve collapses to a point.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Brakke | first = Kenneth A.
 | at = Appendix B, Proposition 2, p. 230
 | isbn = 0-691-08204-9
 | mr = 485012
 | publisher = Princeton University Press, Princeton, N.J.
 | series = Mathematical Notes
 | title = The motion of a surface by its mean curvature
 | url = http://facstaff.susqu.edu/brakke/aux/downloads/papers/motionbook.pdf
 | volume = 20
 | year = 1978}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Chou | first1 = Kai-Seng
 | last2 = Zhu | first2 = Xi-Ping
 | at = Lemma 5.5, p.&nbsp;130, and Section 6.1, pp.&nbsp;144–147
 | doi = 10.1201/9781420035704
 | isbn = 1-58488-213-1
 | location = Boca Raton, Florida
 | mr = 1888641
 | publisher = Chapman & Hall/CRC
 | title = The Curve Shortening Problem
 | year = 2001}}.</ref>

The total absolute curvature may also be defined for curves in three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]. Again, it is at least 2{{pi}} (this is [[Fenchel's theorem]]), but may be larger. If a space curve is surrounded by a sphere, the total absolute curvature of the sphere equals the [[expected value]] of the [[central projection]] of the curve onto a plane tangent to a random point of the sphere.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Banchoff | first = Thomas F. | authorlink = Thomas Banchoff
 | doi = 10.1215/S0012-7094-70-03736-1
 | journal = [[Duke Mathematical Journal]]
 | mr = 0259815
 | pages = 281–289
 | title = Total central curvature of curves
 | volume = 37
 | issue = 2 | year = 1970}}.</ref> According to the [[Fáry–Milnor theorem]], every nontrivial smooth [[Knot (mathematics)|knot]] must have total absolute curvature greater than 4{{pi}}.<ref name="chen"/>
